title: What does the source do regarding him?
question: Gives news of him, steers him, assesses him, calls him out, or only mentions him?
readings: Words as written: if a sentence names who he should fight, that is steering; if it says how he is or when he is back, that is news of him, however hedged or joking.

Firm and aimed at him: an act needs a plain statement about him; a taunt dressed as advice is a callout, a guess ('probably', 'expects') is not news, and a speaker talking about his own next fight is not steering him.

Loudest voice: in an article with several voices (a leak plus fan reaction, a quote plus the hosts' reaction), the act is taken from whichever voice fills most of the text, not from the one that carries the new information.
signals: The sentence says what he should do or who he should fight ('should', 'needs', 'must be next', 'book X vs him'): steers_him or calls_him_out, never news.
The article itself labels the remark as mockery or a provocation ('ironically', 'provoke', 'taunt', 'scoffed'): calls_him_out, not steers_him.
The statement about him is hedged ('probably', 'I guess', 'expects', 'I think they will'): a guess, not a factual update.
Whose next fight does the sentence govern: 'my next fight' (the speaker's own choice) or his?
He is the subject of a stated fact (he is ready, he is recovering, he was booked) rather than named inside what he did for the speaker (he helped me, he invited me).
Question 4 finds a fact. gives_news_of_him is 'someone else's factual update', so with fact no_fact it cannot be right.
With several voices, which one carries the new information about him (the question 2 source)? The act is that voice's act, not the longest voice's.

rules.name: Words as written
rules.text: Take the words as they stand: a sentence naming who he should fight or whether he should rematch is steers_him whatever the tone, and a sentence about his condition, plans, whereabouts or something he did is gives_news_of_him even when hedged or passing. When both appear, steers_him wins.

examples.why: 'Chandler must be next for Topuria' names who he should fight, so steers_him; the article's 'ironically' is ignored.
'Expects him to return next year' is a sentence about his plans, so gives_news_of_him, although it is a guess and fact is no_fact.

rules.name: Firm and aimed at him
rules.text: An act needs a plain statement about him: steers_him or calls_him_out when the speaker says what he should do or who he should fight (calls_him_out when the article itself frames it as mockery or a challenge), and gives_news_of_him only when the speaker states a fact about him, so never when question 4 is no_fact. A guess about him ('probably', 'expects', 'I think'), a speaker's stance on his own next fight ('not my next fight'), a forecast of what the matchmakers will do, or what he did for the speaker (helped me, invited me) is no act: none_of_these.

examples.why: The article says Tsarukyan 'advises ironically' and 'provokes his rival': mockery framed by the text, so calls_him_out.
'Expects him back next year' is hedged and the readers agree there is no fact, so no news of him: none_of_these.

rules.name: Framing sets tone, hedges still count
rules.text: Let the article's own words set the tone: a remark the text calls ironic, mocking or a provocation is calls_him_out; otherwise naming who he should fight, or refusing him a rematch, is steers_him. A statement about his condition or plans is gives_news_of_him even when hedged, and in an article with several voices the act belongs to the voice that carries the new information about him (the question 2 source).

examples.why: The text frames the Chandler line as a provocation, so calls_him_out.
'Expects him back next year' is about his plans, so gives_news_of_him even though it is Pimblett's guess; this is where it parts from the strict rule.

why: It follows the line Anton already drew on facts: a guess about him is not news, so it cannot be 'gives news of him' either, and act stays coherent with question 4 (no fact means no news act). It also uses only words on the page: 'ironically' and 'provoke' on 287 decide callout over steering, and 'expects' on 457 decides guess over news. The cost: a rival's refusal to rematch him, or his guess that he is hurt, lands in none_of_these although it matters to his path; relevance has to come from the other questions, not from act. It also leans on the writer flagging a taunt; a deadpan taunt with no such word will be read as steering.

per_article.287: The text itself calls the Chandler line ironic and a provocation: calls_him_out, not steers_him.
per_article.457: Pimblett 'expects' him back next year and rules out the fight: a guess, no fact, so none_of_these.
per_article.484: 'I don't think that's my next fight' governs Gaethje's fight, and 'probably not until next year, still recovering' is a guess: none_of_these. Note the readers' agreed fact next_fight rests on that same guess, which Anton ruled no fact on #462.
per_article.492: Same two Gaethje lines as 484 inside a long interview about himself: none_of_these.
per_article.516: Tsarukyan says Topuria vs Pimblett 'makes sense' and names the kind of opponent he will get, with no mockery framing: a plain view on who he should fight, steers_him. The forecast about matchmakers alone would be no act.
per_article.883: The new information is Anik's stated fact (the UFC held internal conversations about a rematch), source media: gives_news_of_him. The fans' 'he should fight a contender first' is steering but is not the voice carrying the news.
per_article.975: Donchenko says Amosov helped him and invited him to his gym: about Donchenko's training, nothing stated about Amosov's own state or plans, fact no_fact: none_of_these.
per_article.1045: 'Ready to fight' is quoted flat, not hedged, and the readers find a fact: gives_news_of_him. If the quoted words are his own, it would be speaks_of_himself; the text does not say.
